source: Sohn, Anderson, Reder & Goode (2004) Differential fan effect and attentional focus
finding: Mental-model theory says the focused (organizing) dimension should show a smaller fan effect. ACT-R says larger. The focused dimension showed the larger fan effect. This favours ACT-R's attention-weight account.
numbers: Person-focus group N=19: focused fan slope 98 ms vs 63 ms nonfocused, t(18)=2.59, p<.05. Location-focus group N=17: 118 ms vs 73 ms, t(16)=2.80, p<.05. 28 facts, fan 1-3, 168 targets and 168 foils per person.
limits: Small CMU undergraduate samples. One material type (person-location). The two theories assign the same effect to different dimensions, so material choice matters.
agent_relevance: Attention given to a cue sets how much each extra item hurts. Focusing the agent on a cue makes extra items under it cost more, not less.

source: Sohn et al. (2004) base effect and ACT-R model
finding: Fan effect is replicated across paradigms and stimuli. ACT-R puts it in associative strength S_ji = S - ln(n) and latency T = F*exp(-A). The fan effect holds for foils as well as targets.
numbers: Nonfocused fan effect on accuracy: significant for targets F(2,70)=36.08, p<.0001, not for foils (p>.70). Example RTs: 1,110 ms (fan 1/1) to 1,508 ms (fan 3/3), person focus, targets.
quote: replicated in many different experimental paradigms with different types of stimuli
limits: Foil fan pattern is unexplained by the authors ('not clear at this point why').
agent_relevance: Cost per extra item is logarithmic, so the first extra item hurts most. Going from 1 to 2 items per cue matters more than 10 to 11.

source: Sohn et al. (2004) mental-model rival account
finding: Radvansky and Zacks mental-model theory says facts merged into one model give no fan effect on the organizing dimension. With large locations either dimension can organize and no differential fan appears. With small locations the person fan is smaller.
numbers: Radvansky & Zacks (1991): location fan smaller than object fan for object-location pairs. Radvansky et al. (1993): differential fan with small locations only.
limits: Described second-hand inside the 2004 paper; tested here only through the attention manipulation.
agent_relevance: Merging related items into one coherent record can remove the fan cost. A schema that stores one integrated note per cue may beat many loose notes.

source: Guo, Wu & Yiu (2026) The Interference Gap: Comparing Retrieval Bounds in Human Memory and RAG Systems
finding: Humans and three retrievers all lose accuracy about logarithmically in fan. Humans lose least. Dense passage retrieval loses most. HippoRAG is close to humans on slope.
numbers: Fan slope: human 0.41 [0.35,0.47], DPR 0.67 [0.58,0.76], ColBERTv2 0.53, HippoRAG 0.44 [0.37,0.51]. RAG: 200 entities per fan in {1,2,4,8}, top-1 scored. Humans N=112 (120 minus 8), fan 1,2,4 only. System x fan interaction beta=-0.12, SE .03, p<.001.
quote: Both systems show logarithmic accuracy decline with association count (fan)
limits: Preprint (May 2026). Human fan 8 not tested. Human and RAG formats matched but not identical. Only human vs DPR clearly separated; human CIs overlap HippoRAG and ColBERTv2. Mechanism not identified.
agent_relevance: Accuracy against library size per cue can be modelled as log decline. A graph-indexed library (HippoRAG style) loses less per extra item than a flat embedding index.

source: Guo et al. (2026) human and DPR accuracy by fan
finding: Human recognition accuracy falls with fan from 91.2% to 71.8% over fan 1 to 4. DPR falls from 94.1% to 44.7% over fan 1 to 8.
limits: Prolific online sample, mean age 24.3. 5 s per study sentence, 60 sentences. Single preprint.
agent_relevance: Anchor numbers: doubling items per cue cost a human about 9 points and a dense retriever about 18 points at low fan.

source: Guo et al. (2026) model comparison and false alarms
finding: Log decline beat a power-law alternative in every system. False alarms rise with similarity of competitors, much more for DPR than for humans.
numbers: BIC advantage for log form: 18.4 human, 23.1 DPR, 15.7 HippoRAG; model recovery picked the true model in 94% of cases. False alarms at low similarity: 8.2% human, 12.4% DPR; at high similarity (cos>0.7): 23.1% vs 41.3%. Competitor sensitivity 0.021 human vs 0.058 DPR.
limits: Parameter recovery is on simulated data. Cross-validated R2 .91/.88/.90. Human fits use only 3 fan levels.
agent_relevance: Distinctiveness of items under a cue matters more than their count. Near-duplicate entries are the worst case for a retrieval step.

source: Guo et al. (2026) mechanism discussion
finding: Authors list encoding specificity, temporal context binding and retrieval gating as candidate reasons humans beat DPR. The data cannot tell them apart. HippoRAG may win from graph structure, not hippocampal principles.
numbers: Six falsifiable predictions listed; P1 and P3 supported only for human vs DPR, not vs HippoRAG or ColBERTv2.
limits: Authors state causal attribution is a research programme, not a finding.
agent_relevance: Treat 'cognitive-inspired' retrieval claims as untested. Measure the fan slope of each design.

source: Roberts et al. (2024) Large Language Model Recall Uncertainty is Modulated by the Fan Effect (CoNLL)
finding: Six model families were probed with fan from pretraining and from context. Only Mistral and SOLAR showed clear human-like fan effects in the probability of saying an item is absent. RoBERTa, GPT-2 and Llama-2 showed none; Llama-3 a weak non-significant one.
numbers: Models: RoBERTa, GPT-2, Llama-2, Llama-3, Mistral, SOLAR; each expanded to a PopulationLM of N=50. In-context task recreated Anderson (1974): 26 concepts, 16 fan combinations, lists of 20 persons and 20 places. Threshold r>0.3. Noise floors e.g. Mistral TAG 0.35, SOLAR 0.2.
quote: Our results show that removing uncertainty disrupts the observed effect.
limits: Effects weak next to probability size. Exact r values only in figures. Removing uncertainty removes the effect, so it is not visible in generated text. No lists long enough to test present items in pretraining.
agent_relevance: Fan shows up in token probability, not necessarily in output. Read confidence from probabilities where possible, and do not expect all models to share it.

source: Roberts et al. (2024) in-context differential fan
finding: In context, Mistral showed a stronger person-fan than place-fan correlation, like the human differential fan. SOLAR gave mixed signs: negative with person fan but positive with place fan for absent items.
numbers: Present-item (TPG) correlations reached significance for neither model. Absent-item noise floors 0.3 Mistral and 0.45 SOLAR.
limits: Mixed sign in SOLAR undercuts a clean human match. Small, uncorrected correlation analysis.
agent_relevance: LLM fan is real but model-specific. Measure it per model before designing around it.

source: Analyzing Memory Effects in Large Language Models through the Lens of Cognitive Psychology (2025), fan experiment
finding: GPT-4 recognition of person-location facts falls as fan rises from 1 to 2. Offline Mistral-7B and LLaMA-3-8B show similar trends. Online GPT-4 beats humans on d' at both fans.
numbers: Study list 32 pairs; fan 1 = 32 unique pairs, fan 2 = 16 persons and 16 locations each twice; 64 test items (32 foils). GPT-4 d' about 4.1 (fan 1) and 3.1 (fan 2); human d' from Schneider & Anderson (2012) about 3.7 and 2.5. Accuracy 0.991 to 0.915 in one list-size condition.
quote: The trend of the results showed that increasing the number of associations to an item results in slower retrieval.
limits: No statistical tests or variance for most results. Human vs model d' come from different studies. One online model version. Fan values for the accuracy figures are unclear.
agent_relevance: Fan of 2 already costs about 1 d' unit even for a strong model. Keep facts per cue near 1 where precision matters.

source: Analyzing Memory Effects in LLMs (2025), list length and list strength
finding: Accuracy fell as list size grew from 32 to 40 with some fluctuations. Repeating strong items did not hurt weaker ones (no list-strength effect).
numbers: List size 32 to 40 facts tested. No effect sizes in the text I read.
limits: I read about the first 100,000 of 143,000 characters; the rest was not read.
agent_relevance: Interference in LLMs comes from number of similar items, not from the strength of other items. Duplicating a note does not crowd out others.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference in LLMs (PI-LLM)
finding: When one key is updated many times, accuracy at reading the last value falls roughly log-linearly with number of updates in all models tested. Wrong answers shift from recent stale values to early and made-up values.
numbers: 46 keys, update counts 3 to 400 (log-spaced). Larger models decline slower; at 400 updates mid-size models near 0%. Open-model regression: size class t=3.03, p=.005, N=30; context length t=-0.144, p=.886; R2=.261. Llama-4-maverick near 100% with 2 tracked keys, below 5% with 46.
quote: Once this capacity is taxed by interfering information, retrieval performance degrades inescapably.
limits: Workshop paper (ICML 2025 LCFM). No fit slopes or R2 for curves in the text I read. Absolute accuracy shifts with prompt wording. Reasoning models left out of the regression.
agent_relevance: A cue (key) with many stale values is a direct cue-overload case for context. Keep one current value per key; delete superseded entries.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) mitigations in PI-LLM
finding: Telling the model to forget old values helped little. Chain of thought did not help retrieval. Inserting a fake question-answer turn before the query helped a lot.
numbers: Per-key forget prompt moved accuracy by under 10 points at 100 updates. Mock QA reset: Gemini Flash 2.0 at 150 updates matched baseline at 30-45 updates. CoT equal or worse in 3 of 4 pairs; only Nemotron-Ultra improved and still trailed Nemotron-Super.
limits: CoT tested only up to about 100 updates because of output overflow. Mitigations tested on a subset of models.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'ignore earlier notes' prompts. Structural resets in the context work better, and fit G2 (code, not the model, decides what stays).

source: Wang & Sun (2025) value length and tracked keys
finding: Tracking more keys at fixed input length lowers accuracy log-linearly, and longer values also hurt sharply. Interference is about number of competing items, not just tokens.
numbers: Value length at 20 updates per key: below 40% for every model at 10 words, below 5% at 40 words. Experiment A: 125 or 350 updates per key with 1 to 46 keys.
limits: Synthetic key-value stream, not natural text. Closed-source parameter counts are uncertain.
agent_relevance: Short entries and few tracked items per context beat long ones at equal token count.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The Power of Noise: Redefining Retrieval for RAG Systems (SIGIR)
finding: Adding related but non-answer passages to the gold passage lowers answer accuracy steadily. One distractor already hurts. Attention focuses on the distractor.
numbers: Natural Questions. Llama2 gold-only 0.5642; 1 distractor far from query 0.4733; 8 distractors 0.3106. Declines up to 0.38 (-67%) across models; single distractor up to 0.24 (-25%). ADORE hard-negative distractors: Llama2 0.4068, 0.3815, 0.3626 at 1, 2, 4. Wilcoxon p<.01.
quote: adding just one distracting document causes a sharp reduction in accuracy
limits: Small open models (Llama2, MPT, Phi-2, Falcon), 2K-4K token limits, lenient answer-containment scoring. Not all models decline: MPT rose with distractors (0.2148 to 0.3039 at 8, far).
agent_relevance: Near-miss entries under the same cue cost more than random ones. Filter near-duplicates before they reach the context.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) random documents help
finding: Random unrelated passages did not hurt and sometimes helped when placed next to the query. This is the opposite of fan interference and shows that similarity, not count, drives the cost.
numbers: Llama2 Near position: 0.5642 gold-only, 0.5681 at 6 random, 0.5859 at 14. Far position falls to 0.31-0.37. Closed-book 0.05 to 0.12. In the distractor setting at 18 distractors Llama2: Near 0.37, Far 0.23, Mid 0.17.
limits: Reasons for the gain are not established. Gains of about 4 points for Llama2, not all significant (asterisks). Gold position changes results as much as count.
agent_relevance: Count alone is not the harm. Similar, same-cue items are. Put the key evidence last, nearest the question.

source: Liu et al. (2023/2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Multi-document QA accuracy is U-shaped by position. With many retrieved documents and the answer in the middle, accuracy can fall to near closed-book level.
numbers: Closed-book: GPT-3.5-Turbo 56.1%, Claude-1.3 48.3%, MPT-30B 31.5%, LongChat-13B 35.0%. Oracle: 88.3%, 76.1%, 81.9%, 83.4%. 20 docs, GPT-3.5: index 0 75.8%, index 9 53.8%, index 19 63.2%. Contexts of 10, 20, 30 docs.
quote: performance can degrade significantly when changing the position of relevant information
limits: Position effect, not a pure fan manipulation. 2023-era models. NaturalQuestions and a key-value task.
agent_relevance: Where an item sits matters as much as how many compete. Order retrieved items by importance, best at the ends.

source: Modarressi et al. (2025) NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching (ICML)
finding: When question and needle share almost no words, 11 of 13 long-context models fall below 50% of their short-context score at 32K. Cues with no literal overlap are weak under heavy competition.
numbers: GPT-4o: 99.3% baseline to 69.7% at 32K. 13 models, 58 question-needle pairs, 5 haystacks, 26 placements, 7,540 tests per length. Effective length = longest length above 85% of base score.
limits: Context length and cue overlap vary together, so it is not a pure fan test. Reasoning and CoT variants also declined.
agent_relevance: Cues with few shared tokens with the target are weak. Use explicit literal tags as retrieval cues in the library.

source: Link, van Maanen & Dotlacil (2025) Similarity comes at a cost: fan experiments with semantically related concepts
finding: The fan effect persists when the concepts are semantically similar, in natural Dutch. RTs rise with fan in both experiments. Accuracy loss appeared in only one.
numbers: Exp 1 N=134 (46 lab, 88 online), fan 2 vs fan 4: longer RT and lower accuracy at fan 4. Exp 2 N=97 online, similar concepts: longer RT, accuracy high everywhere (possible ceiling).
limits: Conference poster abstract; Bayesian mixed models; only the abstract page was read. Ceiling in Exp 2.
agent_relevance: Similarity among stored items adds to the cost. Fan costs RT more reliably than accuracy.

source: Reder lab fan effect overview (CMU)
finding: Experts with more knowledge do not slow as fan predicts (the 'paradox of the expert'). Integration of knowledge and retrieval strategy explain part of this. Fan also shows in word-frequency mirror effects and in context features such as font.
numbers: No numeric results on the page. Cites Reder & Anderson (1980), Reder & Ross (1981, 1983), Reder & Wible (1984), Anderson & Reder (1987).
limits: Lab web page, not primary data; numbers need the linked papers.
agent_relevance: Organized, integrated stores avoid fan cost. This supports indexing entries into structured schemas, not flat lists.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Fan effect
finding: Anderson (1974): 26 person-location sentences, slower retrieval for persons paired with more locations. The effect is reduced when random sentences are unified into one concept (Moeser 1979). Retrieval time rises with age (Gerard 1991).
numbers: No RT figures on the page.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, secondary. Does not cover negative fan, integration detail or replication failures.
agent_relevance: Background anchor only.

source: Anderson (1974) Retrieval of propositional information from long-term memory
finding: Founding fan studies. Recognition time rose with the number of locations paired with a person. Not read this session; known through Wikipedia and Sohn et al.
numbers: Wikipedia: three experiments, 26 sentences.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Founding source for the library-size-per-cue idea.

source: Anderson & Reder (1999) The fan effect: New results and new theories (JEP: General)
finding: Spreading activation divided across links, with attention weights per cue; revised after the rival mental-model theory. The source page was not reachable this session.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened. Known only from the Sohn et al. (2004) summary of the ACT-R equation.
agent_relevance: Basis of the log(n) cost used by Guo et al. 2026.

source: Cantor & Engle (1993) Working-memory capacity as long-term memory activation
finding: Low-span people show a larger rise in recognition time with fan. With thematically related sentences, high-span people showed a negative fan effect. Reported by search snippet only.
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Not opened. Snippet from a search result; Bunting et al. (2004) later challenged the capacity reading.
agent_relevance: Capacity may matter: weaker models may show steeper fan slopes (see the PI-LLM size effect).

source: Bunting, Conway & Heitz (2004) Individual differences in the fan effect and working memory capacity (JML)
finding: Four experiments with high- and low-span groups on unrelated sentences. Authors favour attentional control over a general capacity account. Results not retrieved.
numbers: Not retrieved.
limits: Not opened. Abstract-level information from search snippets only.
agent_relevance: Which cue to attend to may matter more than how much can be held.

source: Radvansky & Zacks (1991); Radvansky (1999) mental models vs fan effect
finding: Facts merged into one situation model give no fan effect on the shared dimension. One object across several locations still gives it. A 2002 Chinese replication with changed materials found no fan effect for 'multiple persons have a single object' even with equal spatial-temporal information, which differs from the original.
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Not opened. Search snippets only; the replication claim is from a snippet.
agent_relevance: Integration is a mitigation: group entries under one frame so the cost is paid once.

source: Reder and colleagues, The size of the fan effect: process not representation
finding: Reder argues fan size is set by retrieval processes, not by how information is stored (from a search snippet). The page returned 403.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports controlling the retrieval step, not only the library.

source: Schneider & Anderson (2012) fan effect d' values, as cited in arXiv 2509.17138
finding: Human d' about 3.7 at fan 1 and 2.5 at fan 2, used as the human comparison for GPT-4.
limits: Not opened; second-hand via 2509.17138.
agent_relevance: A human baseline: fan 2 costs about 1.2 d' units.
